introduction: Talk after talk in this guide makes one argument from the wonders of 1912: the phonograph, the telegraph, the electric lamp, the aeroplane and the submarine show that the human mind is not nature’s captive, as the sun and the animals are, and that this discovering power is a spiritual gift meant for a moral end. Sophocles sang the same wonder, Genesis and the eighth psalm speak of dominion, Job’s miner brings hidden things to light, and Whitman and Tennyson greeted the cable and the airship. But the readings’ language of breaking nature’s laws and striking at its heart has had its critics, and they are here too: Bacon, for whom nature is commanded only by being obeyed; Darwin and the Preacher, who doubt that man stands outside nature; Muir, who finds everything hitched to everything else; Thoreau and Emerson, wary of improved means and of things in the saddle; and the Qur’án’s verdict on the creature who took up the trust.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says man “breaks nature’s laws”; Bacon says “nature to be commanded must be obeyed.” Take the aeroplane or the electric lamp: which description fits it better, and does the difference matter to the readings’ conclusion?

“All things are captives of nature except man.” Darwin calls the difference one of degree, and Muir finds everything hitched together. What would the readings lose, and what might they gain, if man were seen as within nature and still responsible for it?
God asks Job, “Canst thou send lightnings?” We now can. How should the old questions meant to humble us be read in an age that has answered some of them?
Thoreau calls inventions “improved means to an unimproved end,” and Emerson says things ride mankind. Where do the readings themselves say what the power over nature is for?
Genesis says both “subdue it” and “dress it and keep it,” and the Qur’án calls the bearer of the trust “a tyrant and a fool.” How would you state the responsibility that goes with the mind’s power?
The readings end with a will that is never satisfied and pearls of the mind that grow forever. How is that restlessness different from the restlessness of acquiring more?

outside.why: Man “soars in the sky, sails upon the ocean and dives beneath it.” The chorus of the Antigone began the list twenty-four centuries earlier: wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man, who crosses the white sea.
“Man through scientific knowledge and power rules nature.” The first chapter of Genesis gives the commission: replenish the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion.
“He has no wings, but he does not submit himself to this fact.” The psalmist had only the wish: oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest.
The telegraph “connects the East and the West.” Whitman greeted the cable and the canal in the same spirit: the earth to be spanned, connected by network, the distant brought near.

The telegraph is offered as proof that man rules nature. Thoreau, when the first lines were going up, called such inventions pretty toys: improved means to an unimproved end. What would count as an improved end?

Sciences, arts and inventions are “emanations of the human mind,” and the people that goes deepest excels. Daniel’s sealed book foresees a time when many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.
What was “in the realm of the unseen” is brought into being. Job’s poem on the miner: he cutteth out rivers among the rocks, and the thing that is hid bringeth he forth to light.
Crafts and sciences were “hidden and concealed mysteries” until discovered. Proverbs: it is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
The rational soul can “penetrate the mysteries of existence.” Aristotle on where the penetrating starts: it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize.
Mysteries “have stepped forth from the invisible plane.” Isaiah’s promise to Cyrus uses the same picture: I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places.
“Everything has been hidden. Man has discovered it.” Xenophanes: the gods have not revealed all things to men from the beginning, but by seeking they find in time what is better.

Nature’s secrets are “made subject to his purposes.” Keats mourned what the explaining costs: there was an awful rainbow once in heaven; we know her woof, her texture. Is anything lost when a mystery is brought into “the realm of the known”?

Man “imprisons” electricity in a lamp and sends messages thousands of miles. God’s question to Job was meant to be unanswerable: canst thou send lightnings, that they may go and say unto thee, Here we are? What follows now that the answer is yes?
Man “discovers the science of aviation and flies in the air like a bird.” Tennyson foresaw it in 1842, commerce in the heavens, and in the same breath the airy navies grappling in the central blue.
“All things are subdued by the hand of man.” The eighth psalm: thou madest him to have dominion over the works of thy hands; thou hast put all things under his feet.

Man alone “can withstand nature” and stands apart from all other beings. John Muir, in the Sierra in 1869, found nothing that stands apart: when we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.

“He breaks nature’s rule” and “contravenes nature’s universal law.” Bacon, the prophet of modern science, described the same mastery differently: nature to be commanded must be obeyed. Does the ship break the law of the sea or use it?
He “traverses the surface of the sea as if it were an open field.” The psalm’s sailors: they that go down to the sea in ships, these see the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.
The sun “is held prisoner in its orbit.” The Qur’án: it is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day; they float each in an orbit.
Nothing in nature “can deviate in the slightest.” The Preacher saw the same fixed round: the sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.

“All things are captives of nature except man.” Darwin concluded that the difference in mind between man and the higher animals, great as it is, is one of degree and not of kind. What in the readings depends on the difference being one of kind?
Even electricity, the most “rebellious and defiant” force, is put to work. The Qur’án: He hath made of service unto you whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth.
Through knowledge man can “strike at nature’s heart.” The oldest story about knowledge in the Bible is a prohibition. Why might a tradition that blesses dominion also tell that story?
“Small in body but vast in thought.” Pascal: man is but a reed, the weakest in nature, but he is a thinking reed; the universe that crushes him knows nothing of it.

Man “rules over nature, rends its laws.” The Qur’án says that the heavens, the earth and the hills shrank from a trust that man took up, and adds its verdict: he hath proved a tyrant and a fool. What goes with the power that the reading celebrates?
The discovering power is “unique to humans,” and by it they are distinguished from animals. Aristotle: reason more than anything else is man.
Humans “are free from nature’s bondage.” The Qur’án addresses those who would pass the bounds of heaven and earth: penetrate them! Ye will never penetrate them save with Our sanction.
All beings “are captive, but humans are free.” The Preacher, looking at death, saw no such difference: a man hath no preeminence above a beast; all go unto one place.

Man has “seized the sword from nature and with it is beating nature back.” Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein learns from his own case how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge. What does her story add to the image of the seized sword?
“Man is ruler over nature, yet man considers himself a prisoner.” Lovelace, writing from an actual prison: stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
The sun’s motion is compelled; man’s is not. Epictetus begins his handbook by marking the one region where that holds: some things are in our control and others not.

“All motion is compelled, not volitional,” except in man. Khayyám will not make the exception: the Moving Finger writes, and having writ, moves on, nor all thy piety nor wit shall lure it back. What do the readings mean by a power “that can break the laws of nature”?

Powers in man “surpass or surround nature.” Kant’s two wonders make the same division: the starry heavens above me, which annihilate my importance as an animal creature, and the moral law within me, which raises my worth.

Man has will; “nature is without will.” Stephen Crane lets nature reply to a man who announces his existence: the fact has not created in me a sense of obligation. Is nature’s indifference a proof of man’s superiority or a limit on it?

“The spirit of man is above the sun.” God’s question to Job: canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades? knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? Which of those questions has changed its answer, and which has not?

Man reads the past from its signs and “deduces what results will emerge in the future.” Thucydides wrote for those who want an exact knowledge of the past as an aid to the understanding of the future.
Columbus found other lands “through his spiritual sense.” Keats’s discoverer stares at the Pacific, and his astronomer sees a new planet swim into his ken.
“The traces of man after his death continue to reveal themselves.” Milton: a good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up on purpose to a life beyond life.
Man “dries up the sea, inundates the desert” and makes nature his prisoner. Genesis tells of builders of whom it was said that nothing would be restrained from them, and what became of their tower.

A forest made into a garden “reverts into its former condition” if neglected. Huxley, Darwin’s defender, used the same garden to argue that ethical progress depends on combating the cosmic process and not on imitating it.
Spirit, mind and soul have each an office. The Katha Upanishad’s chariot: the Self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins.
“The Universal Emperor over the entire body is the Spirit.” Plato’s image of rule within the person is a charioteer with two horses, and he does not pretend that the driving is easy.
“It is mind in the herb and in the mineral.” Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things, all objects of all thought, and rolls through all things.
Illnesses with “a mental origin” are best healed through the mind. Juvenal’s line about what to pray for joins the two: a sound mind in a sound body.

Mind cure for complaints that are mental in their source. Macbeth asks his wife’s doctor to minister to a mind diseased and is told that therein the patient must minister to himself. What can and cannot be done for another’s mind?

If the “luminous aspect” of the intellect overcomes nature, discovery follows. Pope saw the same creature from the other side: born but to die, and reasoning but to err; sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled.
Reason is “the Greatest Bestowal.” Hamlet: he that made us with such large discourse gave us not that capability and godlike reason to fust in us unused.
Human thought is “a mirror of realities.” Zhuangzi: the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror; it grasps nothing, refuses nothing, receives but does not keep.

Control over nature exists so that man may “render effective the will of God.” Before any talk of dominion Genesis gives the first man a humbler charge: to dress the garden and to keep it. What does keeping ask that ruling does not?
“No material power can withstand that mighty force.” Zechariah’s word to a governor facing a mountain of difficulty: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
“How can man be content to lead only an animal existence?” Mill: it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
Man “has been able to conquer” nature’s laws. Emerson looked at the same century and saw the conquest reversed: things are in the saddle, and ride mankind. What decides which way it goes?
A will-power that “will not be satisfied with anything” and spurs its possessor higher. Browning: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for?
“Only the spirit is real; everything else is as shadow.” Paul: the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.

The pearls of the mind can “increase in lustre forever,” unlike those of the sea. Job’s poem, after praising the miner, asks where wisdom shall be found: the depth saith, it is not in me; it cannot be gotten for gold.
